fix.question: In February 1739, a Persian shah of humble nomadic origins routed the Mughal army at Karnal, occupied Delhi, and a month later ordered a massacre that killed tens of thousands. Name this Persian invader of India.
fix.explanation: Nadir Shah Afshar, who rose from a poor herding family in Khorasan to become Shah of Iran, sacked Delhi in March 1739, shattering Mughal prestige and effectively ending Mughal power outside the Doab.

verdicts.notes: Original called Nadir Shah a 'former sheep-herder' — his father was a herdsman; Nader himself sold firewood/wood. Softened to 'humble nomadic origins' to stay accurate.

fix.question: Which fabulously gem-encrusted throne — commissioned by Shah Jahan, inaugurated in 1635 after seven years of work, and carried off to Iran in 1739 as war loot — became so symbolic of Iranian monarchy that later Shahs of Iran were popularly said to sit on it?
fix.explanation: The Takht-i-Tavus was looted by Nadir Shah in 1739; the phrase 'Peacock Throne' came to symbolise the Iranian monarchy, and Pahlavi-era shahs were popularly said to sit on it (though the Pahlavi dynasty's name actually derives from Middle Persian Pahlavi script, not the throne).

verdicts.notes: Original wrongly claimed the throne 'gives its name to the dynasty that later ruled Iran until 1979' — Pahlavi dynasty name comes from Pahlavi script of Middle Persian, NOT from the Peacock Throne. Patched to a softer 'symbolic' framing.

fix.question: Linking Mumbai to Bandar Abbas, on to the Caspian, then up through Russia to Moscow — the multimodal trade corridor that India, Iran and Russia have promoted since 2000 is meant to cut shipping times to Europe roughly in half. Name this corridor, often abbreviated INSTC.

fix.question: Within the Awadhi court the Persian-origin word for the small replica tomb of Imam Husain came to denote both decorative model tombs and the ceremonial structures carried in Muharram processions. Around the time of Muharram, every neighbourhood of Lucknow puts out one of these. Which Persian-origin word?
fix.explanation: Taziya, from the Persian ta'ziyeh (mourning), refers in India to the replica tombs of Imam Husain and the Muharram processions central to Shia Awadhi practice.

verdicts.notes: Original framing 'word for a closed, curtained vehicle' conflated taziya with takht-rawan/palanquin etymologies. Persian ta'ziyeh literally means 'mourning/consolation,' not 'closed vehicle.' Rewrote to standard taziya definition (model tomb/Muharram structure).
